It all comes down to duty cycle and power output.

1. The regulator will (apparently obviously) not charge the battery past its maximum capacity. This is actually a little important to remember because that means if the battery is already full the solar generated power goes exactly nowhere.

  1. Functionally this means that if your battery is fully charged by 1400 it will not receive any more precious electrons until the voltage starts to drop. Unless the usage works out just exactly right you won’t be going into the night with a fully charged battery.

  2. That matters because of duty cycle. Your charger will not put out enough power to “float” the battery. If you doubt this try taking the battery and.out of the system. The point being that the maximum legal output of a CB is 5 watts ERP (effective radiated power) i.e. the strength of the radio frequency signal as measured at the antenna. While this correlates to power drain of the transceiver that 5W does not AT ALL mean you can run 100% of the time on a 7W panel.

You can find the actual current requirements online for most things in their SPECIFICATIONS. But I’m not going to look it up for you now. An even better plan is buy a multimeter - this is something you Willis use continuously; I don’t know how the general public lives without them! A passably usable one is probably < $10. Hook it up in a wire, might as well use the positive one, set it in amp mode and measure it! Key the mic watch it jump. Multiply volts (probably 12-ish) times amps and there is your real number. Extra points for buying an auto ranging meter or setting the scale to MAX and stepping down such that you don’t blow up your precious $10 investment.

Every individual radio will be slightly different. And between models the difference might be somewhat significant.

Last and very important thing to know is the typical solar powered float charger WILL NOT “charge” a battery. It would be entirely possible to suck enough amps out of a battery that the charger refuses to work.

Overall your idea might work. But my gut feel is probably not standalone. You are going to have time when you have to have a real charger. That could absolutely be a car or even a lawnmower with jumper cables. But I wouldn’t want my life to depend on your solar idea alone.

CB radios are power-limited to the antenna output at 5 watts maximum; other electronics would up that power used. I would guesstimate that while transmitting the radio would use about 10 watts. Just leaving the receiver on would need at least 3 or 4 watts and the output to the speaker is 1 or 2 watts. So to use a 7 watt solar panel would limit you to maybe an hour's use per day at best with all things considered. A 7-watt solar panel under optimum sunlight would still give less than 5 watts to the battery. Lead acid batteries are horribly inefficient with losses of 25% or more per charge/discharge. I have 200 watts (200/14=14 amps) on my camper roof and still get only 7+ amps to the battery on a good day due to losses in the controller, etc. Solar panel manufacturers cheat by using the maximum open circuit voltage and the load short circuit current to determine power output. My panels rated at 100 watts have an open circuit output of about 18 volts and about 5 amps into a maximum short circuit load, or 120 watts. With a 7 watt solar panel you would be lucky to get a quarter of an amp to the battery.
